claims.text: Enhanced-sampling free-energy integration accelerated by machine learning can accurately and efficiently determine melting properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
The method determines melting behavior by directly computing and comparing the free-energy landscapes of solid and liquid phases.
The intended initial materials are as-cast or thermally processed polycrystalline HEAs in a homogeneous solid-solution state.
Metadynamics or umbrella sampling can be combined with machine-learning acceleration to calculate complete solid- and liquid-phase free-energy profiles for HEAs.
Applying the method near the melting transition across diverse HEA compositions captures multicomponent effects.
Suitable order parameters can capture lattice configurations and atomic-scale transitions between solid and liquid phases.
Integrating the free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases yields the melting temperature.
The same free-energy calculation yields latent heat, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Machine-learning acceleration efficiently samples the complex configurational space of multicomponent alloys.
The proposed workflow ensures convergence with quantified error margins.
Predicted HEA melting temperatures will be within ±50 K of experimental values.
Predicted fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change will each be within approximately ±5% of measurements across various HEA compositions.

Brute-force molecular dynamics, standard CALPHAD, and first-principles approaches are either prohibitively expensive or lack well-defined quantitative error bounds over the large HEA composition space.
Accuracy will deteriorate when the interatomic potential fails to represent complex multicomponent interactions.
Incomplete enhanced-sampling convergence under extreme configurational fluctuations can reduce reliability.
The ±50 K and ±5% accuracy targets are based on preliminary benchmarks.
In-situ neutron imaging can observe HEA melting, alloying, miscibility, and other liquid-state behavior.
Calorimetry or neutron imaging can provide quantitative experimental values for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting.
The approach is falsified if errors exceed ±50 K for melting temperature or ±5% for any of fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, or melting volume change across the tested compositions.
